claim: The COVID-19 pandemic abruptly upended cancer care in many countries including the US.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic abruptly upended cancer care in many countries including the US.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the following sentences and established knowledge about pandemic impacts.

claim: The need to reduce community spread and reserve hospital capacity for the most severe COVID-19 cases led to rescheduling or postponement of cancer care appointments.
source: The need to reduce community spread and reserve hospital capacity for the most severe COVID-19 cases led to rescheduling or postponement of cancer care appointments (Nelson, 2020; Patt et al., 2020; Ueda et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Wenger et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to scholarly work.

claim: Control measures significantly decreased cancer-related patient encounters in the early phase of the pandemic, particularly for cancer screenings.
source: These control measures significantly decreased cancer-related patient encounters in the early phase of the pandemic, particularly for cancer screenings (Patt et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patt et al., 2020.

claim: Comparing March to July 2020 with the same period in 2019, there was a substantial decrease in cancer screenings, biopsies, surgeries, office visits, and therapy.
source: Comparing March to July 2020 with the same period in 2019, there was a substantial decrease in cancer screenings, biopsies, surgeries, office visits, and therapy; the decreases varied by service location and cancer type (Patt et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patt et al., 2020.

claim: Breast cancer screenings decreased by 89.2% and colorectal by 84.5%.
source: For example, breast cancer screenings decreased by 89.2% and colorectal by 84.5% (Warner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner et al., 2020.

claim: Patients reported delays in receiving cancer care, including follow-up clinic appointments and cancer therapies, such as radiation, infusion therapies, and surgeries.
source: Patients reported delays in receiving cancer care, including follow-up clinic appointments and cancer therapies, such as radiation, infusion therapies, and surgeries (London et al., 2022; Riera et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to London et al., 2022 and Riera et al., 2021.

claim: Cancer care delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic are anticipated to lead to increased cancer morbidity and mortality.
source: Cancer care delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic are anticipated to lead to increased cancer morbidity and mortality (Blay et al., 2021; Malagón et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blay et al., 2021 and Malagón et al., 2022.

claim: An association was found between surgical and screening delays and increased cancer mortality among patients diagnosed with colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer during the pandemic.
source: One study found an association between surgical and screening delays and increased cancer mortality among patients diagnosed with colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer during the pandemic (Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2021.

claim: Delayed mammography and computed tomography for lung cancer were associated with advanced stage of cancer at diagnosis.
source: Delayed mammography and computed tomography for lung cancer were associated with advanced stage of cancer at diagnosis (Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2021.

claim: Delayed surgery for lung cancer was associated with worse survival.
source: Another study determined delayed surgery for lung cancer was associated with worse survival (Mayne et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayne et al., 2021.

claim: Some evidence suggests that patients were reluctant to return for mammograms after care disruptions.
source: For breast screenings, some evidence suggests that patients were reluctant to return for mammograms after care disruptions (Miller et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller et al., 2021.

claim: Cancer care disruptions during COVID-19 could have detrimental future impacts on cancer outcomes and may require changes to public health and clinical strategies across the cancer prevention and control continuum.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about future impacts based on the evidence presented.

claim: Rural communities that already experience limited access to cancer care have less capacity to manage COVID-19.
